questions.question: What is a 'Fork' on GitHub?

options.B: A server-side copy of another user's repository created under your own GitHub account
options.C: A Git command that deletes branches

questions.explanation: Forking creates an independent copy of a repository in your GitHub account, allowing you to freely experiment and push changes without write access to the original.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between `git clone` and forking?

options.A: `git clone` copies a repo to your local computer; forking copies a repo on GitHub servers to your own GitHub account
options.C: Forking only works on private repos
options.D: Cloning costs money, forking is free

questions.explanation: Forking happens on GitHub's cloud platform. Cloning downloads a repository to your local file system.

questions.question: In the open-source fork workflow, what does the remote named `upstream` typically refer to?

options.B: The original parent repository from which you created your fork

questions.explanation: By convention, `origin` points to your personal fork, while `upstream` points to the main project repository.

questions.question: Which command connects the original parent repository as a remote named `upstream`?
questions.explanation: `git remote add upstream <url>` configures the original repo URL so you can pull future updates.

questions.question: How do you fetch the latest commits from the original `upstream` project into your local machine?
questions.explanation: `git fetch upstream` downloads the newest branches and commits from the main project into your local cache.

questions.question: Why can't you push commits directly to a popular open-source repository like `facebook/react`?

options.A: Because Git only allows one commit per day
options.B: Because you do not have write/push permissions to that repository; you must fork it and submit a Pull Request instead
options.C: Because React is not written in Git
options.D: Because pushing to public repos requires a paid license

questions.explanation: Public repositories only grant write access to core maintainers. External contributors contribute via forks and pull requests.

questions.question: How can you keep your local `main` branch synchronized with changes made to `upstream/main`?

options.A: `git switch main && git pull upstream main`

questions.explanation: Pulling from `upstream main` merges the latest official commits into your local main branch.

questions.question: Does GitHub provide a web button to sync your fork directly without using terminal commands?

options.A: No, it is strictly command-line only
options.B: Yes, GitHub has a 'Sync fork' button on your fork's repository homepage
options.D: Only if you have fewer than 10 commits

questions.explanation: GitHub's web UI features a 'Sync fork' dropdown that allows you to update your fork's branch with one click.

questions.question: When you push commits to your fork's `origin`, does that automatically change the original author's repository?

options.A: Yes, all forks automatically alter the original project
options.B: No, your fork is completely isolated until you submit a Pull Request and the maintainers approve and merge it
options.C: Only if you push to the main branch

questions.explanation: Your fork is your private playground. Nothing touches the upstream repository without an approved Pull Request.

questions.question: What is the recommended branch to create when working on a bug fix in your fork?

options.A: Always commit directly on `main` in your fork
options.B: Create a dedicated feature or fix branch (e.g. `fix/typo-in-docs`) so your PR is clean and isolated

questions.explanation: Creating dedicated branches on your fork makes opening clean, focused Pull Requests simple and avoids polluting your fork's `main` branch.
